1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6.background: The more “tactical” of the two main branches of the Scandinavian Defence, known as the Modern Scandinavian. John Emms calls 3.d4 White's main line against it.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: The main line. White gives up the idea of keeping the pawn and takes central space instead, opening lines for the queen and the c1-bishop. Black wins the pawn back, so the game turns on whether White's bigger centre outweighs Black's quick, comfortable development.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4.strategy: Defends the d5 pawn with a pawn and tries to keep the extra material instead of handing it back. The cost is that the c4 pawn blocks the f1-bishop's diagonal and gives Black a target: the pawn chain can be chipped away at once, and White often has to return the pawn anyway.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 c6.strategy: The most common reply: the c-pawn attacks d5 from the side and aims to open the centre. If White grabs on c6, Black recaptures with a knight and has a lead in development for the pawn, so White normally returns the pawn with a central strike, which gives an equal game.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 c6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Panov Transfer

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6.strategy: A gambit for speed: if White takes on e6, Black's bishop recaptures with development and hits the c4 pawn. Black hopes that an open position and a lead in development outweigh the pawn, but against calm play it is simply a pawn down.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Icelandic-Palme Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6.background: Invented by Icelandic masters who looked for an alternative to the more common 3...c6.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5.name: Scandinavian Defence: Marshall Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5.strategy: The natural reply: Black wins the pawn back at once with a knight that is already developed, so no time is lost. The knight stands in the centre but can be driven off by c4 while White builds a bigger centre, so Black has to avoid ending up cramped.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4.background: The line had some popularity in the late 1990s. According to a monograph by Roush, Lance and Cornell, John Donaldson christened it in 1996, recognising several Portuguese players; David Smerdon calls the name a little unfair to earlier exponents such as the Belgian IM Michel Jadoul.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4.strategy: Develops with an attack on the queen and does not hurry to recapture. White can keep the extra pawn, so this is a real gambit: Black bets on quick development and active pieces, and the game is sharp from the start.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6.strategy: A less direct way to regain the pawn: the c-pawn attacks d5 a third time and keeps Black's set-up compact, but it spends a move on a pawn instead of developing a piece. Sound, but Black is a step behind in development compared with the main reply.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Richter Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6.background: A rare move that IM Kurt Richter played on occasion in the 1930s.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6.strategy: A rare fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will press on d4 from a distance instead of developing in front of White's central pawns. Black leaves d5 alone for the moment, so White can secure the extra pawn and the space with c4.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3.strategy: The main move: it parries the threat to the queen and attacks the bishop at once. The cost is that f3 takes the natural square from the g1-knight and loosens the king's side, so White must castle before the centre opens, since Black is ahead in development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Nf3.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Classical Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Nf3.strategy: Meets the threat by developing a piece and does not weaken the kingside, bringing White closer to castling. The bishop pins the knight to the queen for now, but the pin is easily undone once the f1-bishop develops; the price is that the d5 pawn is offered back.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+.strategy: A check inserted before the queen is saved: Black must answer it, and the d5 pawn, which controls c6, makes one of the natural blocks risky. The threat to the queen stays, so White still has to deal with it afterwards, having used the tempo to shape how Black blocks.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Be2.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Wuss Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Be2.strategy: Sidesteps the threat by offering a bishop trade. After it Black recovers the d5 pawn with the queen, so White gives the pawn back for a quiet, safe position; it is harmless, since it asks nothing of Black's active development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ Nbd7.strategy: The usual block: the b8-knight develops and the pawn structure stays untouched. The knight is pinned to the king for now, so Black may chase the bishop away later. The threat to the queen has not gone away, so White still has to find an answer.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ c6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Elbow Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ c6.strategy: Blocks the check with the pawn and offers it. Taking the queen at once is a mistake: after dxc6 Bxd1? the discovered check c7+ wins material back with interest. Recapturing with the knight instead gives Black development for a pawn at best.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5.strategy: Keeps the bishop active on the b1-h7 diagonal instead of retreating passively, accepting that f3 has gained a tempo on it. White's f3 has not developed a piece and has loosened the king's side, so Black's lead in development remains the point and Black plays to open the centre before White castles.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ Nbd7.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Lusophobe Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ Nbd7.strategy: Meets the threat to the queen with a retreat, but the check has achieved little: Black has put the b8-knight on d7 in the process and can trade bishops and take back the pawn. White has spent two moves with the bishop, so this is a harmless line rather than a try for an edge.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.g.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Correspondence Refutation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.g.strategy: The sharpest answer: the pawn hits the bishop again and prepares g5 against the f6-knight, gaining space and time while White keeps the pawn. Black's lead in development is hard to use because the knight is pushed to a passive square; the price is a loosened kingside.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.c.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Banker Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.c.background: In David Smerdon's telling, GM Zili Wang played it against Rui Damaso in a Portugal-China match in Macao in 1996 and was checkmated in thirteen moves.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.c.strategy: Secures the d5 pawn with a pawn and so holds the extra material. The price is time: the c4 pawn shuts in the f1-bishop, development is unfinished, and the centre can be opened up against the uncastled king, so White must not grab too much while behind in development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.strategy: Checks first so that Black must put a piece in front of the king, with the d5 pawn controlling c6 and making one block awkward. White then supports d5 with the c-pawn, having developed the bishop with tempo, though on b5 it can be attacked by a pawn.

The usual block: it develops the b8-knight and keeps the c-pawn free. The knight is pinned to the king for now, so Black needs to chase the bishop away to free it, while White's task is to secure the d5 pawn before Black's lead in development tells.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Jadoul Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.strategy: Secures the d5 pawn with a pawn, so Black cannot win it back easily while the knight on d7 is pinned. White holds the extra pawn and a space advantage, but the position is loose around the king, and Black plays for a central pawn break to open the game.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Melbourne Shuffle Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.strategy: Defends d5 with a piece and develops, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, so no pawn supports d5. It holds the pawn less firmly than a pawn would and gives Black targets for piece play, while White keeps the extra pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6.strategy: Takes a second pawn, but Black recaptures with a piece or counters in the centre and gets a lead in development and open lines for the pawns. White has to defend the extra material with the king still in the centre, which is risky.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 e5.name: Scandinavian Defence: Kádas Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 e5.strategy: A further pawn offered: Black attacks d4 at once and opens the diagonal of the f8-bishop, betting that open lines and a lead in development outweigh the material. White must then complete development with the king still in the centre, so Black has real chances if White is careless.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.c4.strategy: The natural reply: the c-pawn defends d5 and takes space, so White keeps the extra pawn, which the fianchetto cannot regain quickly. White builds a broad pawn centre, and Black has to undermine it with pieces and pawn breaks.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.c4 b5.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation, Wing Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.c4 b5.strategy: A second pawn sacrificed: the b-pawn attacks the c4 pawn that guards d5, hoping to win d5 back with a gain of time. After cxb5 Black regains that pawn, but is still a pawn down with only pressure on the long diagonal as compensation.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4.strategy: Drives the knight away with a gain of time and builds a broad centre. Black must retreat the knight and fight for a share of it; White gets a space advantage, at the price of a slightly shut-in f1-bishop and a c4 pawn that becomes a target.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and defends d4, choosing piece development over chasing the knight at once. The pawn push to c4 can follow, but meanwhile Black has time to develop the c8-bishop outside the pawn chain.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4 Nb4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Kiel Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4 Nb4.background: Rarely seen in practice because it is difficult to play effectively; Harman and Taulbut call it "a speculative try".
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4 Nb4.strategy: A speculative try: the knight hits c2 and d3, hoping for Qa4+ N8c6 d5? b5! with a good game. But White simply drives it back with a3, gaining time and space, so Black has spent two moves with the same knight for nothing.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 Bg4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation, Gipslis Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop before it is shut in by ...e6 and pins the f3-knight to the queen, so White's centre loses a defender if the knight is taken. Black aims to catch up in development before White's space tells.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Richter Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto aimed at d4. White gains time with c4 against the knight on d5 and builds a big centre, while Black has the long-term pressure of the bishop as compensation; sound, but White's space is easy to play with.
